The repo is a single-file crate (`src/lib.rs`); the new commits since the last review add the empty-slice guard to `average` and the new `first` function.

**What the new commits do:**
- They fix the previously kept, posted finding `f-divide-by-zero`: `average` now returns 0 for an empty slice and the doc comment matches. I'm marking that finding as fixed.
- They add `first(items, n)`, which slices `&items[..n]` with no bounds clamping. Unlike its sibling `last` (which uses `saturating_sub` and documents "or all of them when there are fewer"), `first` panics for any `n > items.len()` — e.g. `first(&[1, 2, 3], 5)`. That's the main remaining problem.
- Separately, the `i32` sum inside `average` can overflow on realistic inputs (a few million values around 1000 already exceed `i32::MAX` when summed): a debug build panics and a release build silently wraps to a wrong answer.

I am not re-raising the dropped `f-integer-division` finding, since the new commits didn't change that behavior.

draftedFindings.title: first() panics when n exceeds the slice length
draftedFindings.body: `&items[..n]` requires `n <= items.len()`, so `first(&[1, 2, 3], 5)` panics. The sibling `last()` deliberately avoids this via `items.len().saturating_sub(n)` and documents "or all of them when there are fewer", so `first` is both inconsistent and a trap for plausible call sites. Fix by clamping: `&items[..items.len().min(n)]`, and mirror `last`'s doc comment.

draftedFindings.title: average() can overflow the i32 sum
draftedFindings.body: `items.iter().sum::<i32>()` panics on overflow in debug builds and silently wraps in release, yielding a wrong average. This is reachable with realistic data: a few million values around 1000 already exceed `i32::MAX` when summed. Consider summing in `i64` (e.g. `items.iter().map(|&x| i64::from(x)).sum::<i64>() / items.len() as i64`, cast back to `i32`) or documenting the overflow behavior.
